screens.title: OSPF Troubleshooting and Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter prepares you to find and fix the most common OSPF problems and to make targeted optimizations that improve convergence and path selection. You will learn how adjacency failures occur, how to inspect the link-state database for flood or consistency issues, and how to use the Junos suite of show commands as your first line of diagnosis. We also cover deeper debugging with traceoptions and live packet observation with monitor traffic so you can see OSPF packets and state transitions in real time. Finally, you will practice optimization knobs such as interface cost, interface priority for DR/BDR elections, and timer tuning, and learn best practices like consistent reference-bandwidth and stable router IDs. An emphasis runs through the chapter on safe debugging: enable traceoptions briefly and capture the problem, then remove debug configuration. By the end, you will be able to locate the cause of a flapping adjacency, confirm LSDB consistency, and adjust costs or timers in a controlled way to improve path choice and stability. Consider how these skills help reduce outages and speed incident resolution.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the most frequent OSPF failure modes, use Junos "show" commands to confirm neighbor states and database contents, and run targeted debugging that safely collects packet and state information. You will configure and remove traceoptions to capture hello and LSA events, and you will use monitor traffic to inspect live OSPF packets on interfaces. You will also learn optimization techniques: setting interface cost to influence path selection, changing interface priority to control DR/BDR outcomes, and adjusting hello and dead timers when faster convergence is required. Importantly, you will learn a set of operational best practices, such as keeping a consistent reference-bandwidth, using loopback router IDs for stability, and documenting summarization and redistribution rules. For each objective you will see why it matters and a small mnemonic or visual cue to remember the action. These objectives combine diagnosis, controlled debugging, and conservative optimization so you can both fix problems quickly and avoid creating new ones.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to diagnostic commands and debugging, you will practice operational tasks that prevent future problems. You will learn to set a stable router ID using loopbacks, to configure consistent reference-bandwidth so interface costs are meaningful on high-speed links, and to apply area types and summarization to limit LSA flooding and SPF overhead. You will practice changing interface priorities to control who becomes DR and BDR on shared segments, and you will verify effects with show ospf neighbor and show route protocol ospf. Finally, you will be able to document the changes and clean up debugging artifacts. Each of these applied objectives emphasizes minimal disruption: change one parameter at a time, verify behavior, and roll back if undesired. Through hands-on steps you will see how a single mismatched timer or MTU can cause repeated adjacency flaps, and how a small cost change can prefer one path over another. These skills are essential to keeping a production OSPF domain predictable and manageable.

screens.title: Adjacency Formation: Causes and Diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: Adjacency formation is the process by which two OSPF routers negotiate enough shared parameters to exchange routing information. A stable adjacency reaches Full state and allows DBD, LSAs, and subsequent SPF work to proceed. Common causes of failure include mismatched area IDs, mismatched authentication (type or keys), different network types (for example one side thinking it's point-to-point while the other is broadcast), hello and dead timer mismatches, MTU differences, and subnet misconfiguration. When a neighbor is stuck in states such as Init, 2-Way, or ExStart, check these exact parameters. A concrete example: if R1 and R2 are connected on ge-0/0/0.0 and R1 has hello-interval 5 while R2 uses 10, R2 will see inconsistent timing and the adjacency may never progress to Full. A common misconception is to assume interface up/down is enough; a link can be up at L2 but still fail adjacency due to timer or MTU mismatch. To diagnose, run show ospf neighbor and show ospf interface detail to compare states and configured parameters. After you identify the mismatch, change one parameter, commit, and verify; avoid multiple simultaneous changes. What single mismatch would you check first on a flapping adjacency?

keyIdea.title: Match parameters to form Full
keyIdea.text: Mismatched hello/dead timers, MTU, auth, area ID, or network type are the prime causes of adjacency failure.

content.html:
Core Concept › Adjacency Formation
Adjacency causes
  • Area ID mismatch — routers think they are in different areas and will not form adjacency.
  • Authentication mismatch — differing auth type or keys prevents hello acceptance.
  • Timer mismatch — hello/dead intervals must match or adjacency fails.
  • MTU mismatch — ExStart/DBD exchanges fail if MTU differs.
  • Network type mismatch — broadcast vs point-to-point affects DR election behavior.
Example
R1 hello 5s vs R2 hello 10s causes adjacency to stall; fix by matching timers.
Misconception
Link up at L2 does not guarantee adjacency if OSPF parameters differ.
Diagnosis checklist
show ospf neighbor
Confirm neighbor state, interface, ID and priority.
show ospf interface <if> detail
Compare hello/dead, cost, auth, network type and MTU.
Practical check
Change one parameter at a time, commit, and observe neighbor state transitions.
Key Takeaway

Use show commands to compare configuration and runtime details; mismatches are usually the cause.

screens.title: Essential show commands for OSPF diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable troubleshooting workflow begins with a small set of show commands that reveal OSPF state from different perspectives. Start with show ospf neighbor to confirm which neighbors exist and their states; a neighbor not in Full signals a problem. Then run show ospf interface detail to inspect hello and dead intervals, network type, cost, authentication, and MTU on that interface. Use show ospf database to validate LSAs and confirm whether expected router, network, summary, or external LSAs are present; filtering by LSA type narrows the view. Next, show route protocol ospf reveals what routes the router installed from OSPF and their metrics, which helps confirm whether SPF produced the expected result. Finally, show ospf statistics helps you detect packet-level issues such as missing or excessive hello or LSAs. A concrete example: when you suspect an adjacency failure between R1 and R2, run show ospf neighbor repeatedly to see state progression, then use show ospf interface detail to compare the configured hello-interval on both ends. Keep output capture or logs and correlate timestamps. A common mistake is to only check the routing table; always verify neighbors and database consistency first.

keyIdea.title: Evidence-first workflow
keyIdea.text: Confirm neighbor state, interface parameters, LSDB contents, and installed routes in that order to form a diagnosis.

content.html:
Definition › Show Commands Walkthrough
Commands to run
show ospf neighbor
Verify neighbor ID, interface, state and priority.
show ospf interface <int> detail
Compare hello, dead, cost, auth, network type, and MTU.
show ospf database [type]
Confirm LSAs exist and propagate as expected.
show route protocol ospf
Check which routes were installed and their metrics.
show ospf statistics
Look for missing hellos or excessive LSAs which indicate flaps or storms.
Code examples
show ospf neighbor
show ospf interface ge-0/0/0.0 detail
show ospf database router
show ospf database summary
show route protocol ospf
show ospf statistics
Pro tip
Capture outputs with timestamps and compare across routers; this creates reliable evidence when troubleshooting intermittent issues.

screens.title: traceoptions: capture OSPF events safely
screens.narratorSegment: Traceoptions lets you log detailed OSPF activity to a file on Junos, including hello events, LSA processing, packet exchange, and state changes. Use traceoptions when show commands and monitor traffic do not reveal the timing or content of problem events. A safe workflow: configure a small file size and limited flags, reproduce the issue or wait for it to occur, review the log with show log, then delete the traceoptions configuration. Example configuration steps show how to limit impact: set protocols ospf traceoptions file ospf-debug size 1m files 2, then enable specific flags such as hello, lsa, packet, error, or state. After collecting logs, run show log ospf-debug and inspect timestamps and messages that indicate hello mismatches, dropped packets, or SPF recalculations. Remember that leaving traceoptions enabled can consume C P U and disk, so always remove them after verification. A common misconception is that more flags are always better; in production, prefer targeted flags to avoid overwhelming logs. When you do enable extensive tracing in a lab or maintenance window, monitor C P U and log size. What specific flag would you enable first to confirm hello interval problems?

keyIdea.title: Controlled trace capture
keyIdea.text: Enable only the flags you need, capture the event, analyze the ospf-debug log, then delete traceoptions to avoid performance impact.

content.html:
Process Flow › traceoptions Workflow
Configure traceoptions
set protocols ospf traceoptions file ospf-debug size 1m files 2
set protocols ospf traceoptions flag hello detail
set protocols ospf traceoptions flag error
set protocols ospf traceoptions flag state
commit
Limit file size and flags to reduce resource usage. Use detail for verbose hello output only when needed.
Inspect and clean up
After reproducing the issue, run:
show log ospf-debug | last 50
delete protocols ospf traceoptions
commit
Common mistake
Leaving traceoptions enabled in production can fill disk and increase CPU; always delete when done.
Key Takeaway

Traceoptions are powerful but must be used briefly and with targeted flags to avoid impacting device resources.

screens.title: monitor traffic: observing OSPF on the wire
screens.narratorSegment: When log messages do not reveal the problem, a packet capture on the interface lets you observe the actual OSPF packets exchanged. Junos monitor traffic interface detail can capture live packets similar to a tcpdump. You can filter for OSPF so you only see hellos, database description packets, and LSAs. For example, monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0.0 no-resolve layer-2-headers matching "ospf" will show you whether hellos are being transmitted and which neighbor addresses they contain. Use this to verify that timers, authentication, and source addresses are correct from both ends. A practical use: if hellos arrive but DBDs never follow, inspect the DBD flags and sequence numbers — this can indicate MTU or DBD master/slave negotiation issues. One misconception is to rely solely on captured packet presence; you must inspect fields such as authentication or network type to confirm compatibility. After capturing, stop the monitor and correlate packet timestamps with show logs to form a full timeline. Which packet exchange would you capture to diagnose ExStart issues? monitor traffic: observing OSPF on the wire means use monitor traffic with an ospf filter to confirm what is sent and what the neighbor receives; inspect packet fields for mismatches.. In practical terms, capture live packets to verify hellos, dbd exchanges, and lsa floods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › monitor traffic
Live capture example
monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0.0 no-resolve layer-2-headers matching "ospf"
Look for hello source addresses, authentication info, DBD flags and sequence numbers, and LSA headers to verify correct exchanges.
When to use
  • Intermittent adjacency flaps that don't show a clear pattern in logs.
  • DBD exchange failures such as ExStart/Exchange that imply MTU or master/slave issues.
  • Confirming that hellos carry the expected parameters like area and auth.
Misconception
Seeing packets on the wire does not prove the neighbor accepted them; always cross-check with show ospf neighbor and LSDB contents.
Key Takeaway

Use monitor traffic to corroborate what is sent and what is received; correlate captures with logs for a complete timeline.

screens.title: LSA Flooding and LSDB consistency
screens.narratorSegment: LSA flooding is how OSPF distributes topology information. Routers flood LSAs within an area so each router maintains a consistent link-state database. Problems occur when some routers do not receive LSAs or have stale LSAs, producing inconsistent LSDBs and different SPF results. Symptoms include missing summary or external routes on some routers, or asymmetric path choices. Diagnosis starts with show ospf database and filtering by LSA type to see if expected router, network, summary, or external LSAs are present. Compare the LSDB on two neighbors for the same LSAs and sequence numbers; an older sequence number suggests the LSA did not flood correctly. Common causes of flooding problems are interface adjacency failures, area misconfiguration, or filters that block LSA types. An example: if an ASBR advertises an external LSA but some internal routers lack that LSA, run show ospf database external on multiple routers to find where flooding stopped. A misconception is to assume that a single missing route in the routing table is a distribution problem; first confirm whether the LSDB itself is inconsistent. How would you quickly confirm where an LSA stopped propagating?

keyIdea.title: Confirm LSDB consistency
keyIdea.text: Use show ospf database on multiple routers and compare LSA types and sequence numbers to locate flooding gaps.

content.html:
Comparison › LSA Flooding & LSDB
LSA consistency checks
  • Run show ospf database [type] on multiple routers and compare LSAs and sequence numbers.
  • Look for missing LSAs, lower sequence numbers, or LSAs aged out only on some routers.
  • Check for filters, area type mismatches, and adjacency issues on routers that lack LSAs.
Example
An external LSA from an ASBR appears on the ABR but not on some internal routers — inspect ABR and downstream adjacencies for flood blockage.
Quick commands
show ospf database router
show ospf database network
show ospf database summary
show ospf database external
Misconception
Missing route in the routing table is not proof of LSDB inconsistency; verify the LSDB first before changing policies.
Key Takeaway

Compare LSDBs across routers and use sequence numbers to find where flooding stopped; fix adjacencies or filters accordingly.

screens.title: Incorrect route calculations: causes and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: When OSPF adjacencies and LSDBs are consistent but routing still looks wrong, the issue is often cost, summarization, or redistribution. OSPF selects routes based on cost; if interface costs are misconfigured or reference-bandwidth differs across routers, equal links may show different costs and lead to unexpected path selection. For example, older default reference-bandwidth values can make 10Gbps links appear identical to 100Mbps links if not set consistently, which can dramatically change preferred paths. Summarization at ABRs reduces LSDB size but can hide specific prefixes and affect path selection; incorrect summary ranges or accidental overlaps can lead to suboptimal routes. Redistribution of external routes must be done carefully because external LSAs have different cost semantics and type; multiple ASBRs require careful metrics to control preferencing. To fix route calculation issues, verify reference-bandwidth settings domain-wide, inspect configured interface costs with show ospf interface detail, and review ABR summarization and redistribution configuration. A misconception is assuming only adjacency problems change routes; cost and summarization are frequent silent culprits. What would you check first if a network path suddenly prefers a longer physical route?

keyIdea.title: Costs and summaries matter
keyIdea.text: Check reference-bandwidth and interface costs first, then review summarization and redistribution that affect SPF results.

content.html:
Comparison › Route Calculation
Causes
  • Reference-bandwidth mismatch causing inconsistent default costs on fast links.
  • Manual interface cost misconfiguration altering SPF preferences.
  • Summarization hiding more specific prefixes and changing path selection.
  • Redistribution metrics causing external LSAs to be preferred.
Example
Set reference-bandwidth consistently; otherwise a 10Gb link may have the same cost as a 100Mbps link under default settings.
Fix checklist
  1. Check show ospf interface detail to see interface cost.
  2. Confirm domain-wide reference-bandwidth setting and align it on all routers.
  3. Review ABR summarization ranges and redistribution metrics.
  4. Make one change at a time and verify show route protocol ospf results.
Misconception
Assuming physical bandwidth alone determines path selection; OSPF uses configured cost derived from reference-bandwidth and manual overrides.
Key Takeaway

When routes change unexpectedly, verify costs and summarization before assuming a connectivity fault elsewhere.

screens.title: Interface Cost and Reference-Bandwidth
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF uses a numeric cost metric to choose best paths; lower cost is preferred. Junos typically derives cost from a reference-bandwidth divided by the interface bandwidth, but you can override cost per interface. When networks include high-speed links, inconsistent reference-bandwidth settings can make the default costs meaningless — for example, the classic case where the default 100Mbps reference makes a 10Gb link and a 100Mbps link appear proportionally similar. To influence routing deterministically, set reference-bandwidth consistently across the OSPF domain and use manual interface cost for special path control. A concrete command example is set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0 cost 10 to prefer a path. A common operational pitfall is changing costs on only some routers; always apply reference-bandwidth globally and document manual costs. When testing, use show ospf interface detail and show route protocol ospf to verify the effect. The closing question to consider: if an alternative path is still chosen after adjusting cost, what other OSPF or platform-specific factors might influence the decision? Interface Cost and Reference-Bandwidth means use consistent reference-bandwidth and manual interface cost to make path selection predictable across the domain.. In practical terms, how cost influences path selection and why consistent reference-bandwidth matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reference-bandwidth

Manual cost

Use manual costs for traffic-engineering where simple metrics suffice.

screens.title: Interface Priority and DR/BDR elections
screens.narratorSegment: Interface priority influences the Designated Router and Backup Designated Router election on multi-access networks. The router with the highest priority wins the DR role; a priority of 0 prevents a router from becoming DR or BDR. Use interface priority to ensure predictable DR placement on broadcast segments, which can reduce unnecessary topology churn. For example, set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0 priority 100 to favor a particular router as DR. A common scenario: on a hub-and-spoke LAN, you may prefer the hub switch or router to be the DR to centralize LSDB origin and reduce transient master/slave issues. Definition › Interface Priority
Priority controls DR election
Higher priority wins DR election on broadcast or NBMA segments. Priority 0 prevents a router from becoming DR or BDR.

Operational notes

  • Change priorities carefully to avoid unnecessary re-elections.

screens.title: OSPF Timers: hello and dead intervals
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF hello and dead intervals determine how quickly neighbors detect each other and detect failures. Defaults for broadcast networks are typically 10 seconds for hello and 40 seconds for dead. You can decrease these intervals to achieve faster detection and convergence — useful for time-sensitive services like voice — but aggressive settings increase hello churn and C P U load from more frequent SPF runs and LSA flooding. Mismatched timers are a very common cause of adjacency failures, so ensure both ends of a link use the same values. Example configuration to speed detection: set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0 hello-interval 5 and dead-interval 20. When you change timers, monitor C P U and LSA counts with show ospf statistics and observe whether SPF runs increase. A misconception is to tune timers globally without understanding link stability; prefer per-interface tuning in controlled sections of the network where you need faster failure detection. After any timer change, run show ospf neighbor and show ospf interface detail to confirm adjacency stability. What metrics would you watch to make sure faster timers do not overwhelm a router?

keyIdea.title: Balance speed and stability
keyIdea.text: Tune hello and dead intervals only when needed; monitor CPU and LSA activity to avoid increased instability.

content.html:
Process Flow › OSPF Timers
Timer tuning example
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0 hello-interval 5
set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0 dead-interval 20
Tuning reduces detection time but increases control traffic and potential SPF runs; monitor resource usage after change.
When to tune

  • Not recommended across unstable or lossy links where flaps could amplify problems.

Faster timers are always better; in reality they increase control-plane load and LSA churn and must be tested carefully.

Tune hello and dead intervals selectively, monitor CPU and show ospf statistics for increased LSA or SPF activity after changes.

screens.title: Best practices to maintain a stable OSPF network
screens.narratorSegment: A set of operational best practices prevents many OSPF problems before they happen. First, use a consistent reference-bandwidth across the OSPF domain so interface costs compare correctly. Second, run loopbacks for router IDs to keep IDs stable even when physical interfaces flap. Third, enable authentication such as MD5 or SHA for production to avoid unauthorized LSA injection. Fourth, minimize the number of ABRs and ASBRs when possible; each adds SPF and LSDB complexity. Fifth, avoid virtual links unless necessary, and document their temporary nature. Sixth, summarize routes at ABRs to reduce LSDB size and SPF overhead, particularly in large networks. Seventh, document all OSPF design decisions, interface costs, priorities, and timer changes so future engineers can reproduce and audit configurations. Finally, always remove traceoptions and temporary monitoring configurations after troubleshooting to preserve device resources. A misconception is that adding more ABRs automatically improves resilience; instead, each ABR increases the domain's complexity. Which two practices would you prioritize on a network with frequent SPF spikes? This chapter prepares you to find and fix the most common OSPF problems and to make targeted optimizations that improve convergence and path selection. You will learn how adjacency failures occur, how to inspect the link-state database for flood or consistency issues, and how to use the Junos suite of show commands as your first line of diagnosis. We also cover deeper debugging with traceoptions and live packet observation with monitor traffic so you can see OSPF packets and state transitions in real time. Finally, you will practice optimization knobs such as interface cost, interface priority for DR/BDR elections, and timer tuning, and learn best practices like consistent reference-bandwidth and stable router IDs. An emphasis runs through the chapter on safe debugging: enable traceoptions briefly and capture the problem, then remove debug configuration. By the end, you will be able to locate the cause of a flapping adjacency, confirm LSDB consistency, and adjust costs or timers in a controlled way to improve path choice and stability. Consider how these skills help reduce outages and speed incident resolution.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the most frequent OSPF failure modes, use Junos "show" commands to confirm neighbor states and database contents, and run targeted debugging that safely collects packet and state information. You will configure and remove traceoptions to capture hello and LSA events, and you will use monitor traffic to inspect live OSPF packets on interfaces. You will also learn optimization techniques: setting interface cost to influence path selection, changing interface priority to control DR/BDR outcomes, and adjusting hello and dead timers when faster convergence is required. Importantly, you will learn a set of operational best practices, such as keeping a consistent reference-bandwidth, using loopback router IDs for stability, and documenting summarization and redistribution rules. For each objective you will see why it matters and a small mnemonic or visual cue to remember the action. These objectives combine diagnosis, controlled debugging, and conservative optimization so you can both fix problems quickly and avoid creating new ones.

In addition to diagnostic commands and debugging, you will practice operational tasks that prevent future problems. You will learn to set a stable router ID using loopbacks, to configure consistent reference-bandwidth so interface costs are meaningful on high-speed links, and to apply area types and summarization to limit LSA flooding and SPF overhead. You will practice changing interface priorities to control who becomes DR and BDR on shared segments, and you will verify effects with show ospf neighbor and show route protocol ospf. Finally, you will be able to document the changes and clean up debugging artifacts. Each of these applied objectives emphasizes minimal disruption: change one parameter at a time, verify behavior, and roll back if undesired. Through hands-on steps you will see how a single mismatched timer or MTU can cause repeated adjacency flaps, and how a small cost change can prefer one path over another. These skills are essential to keeping a production OSPF domain predictable and manageable.

Adjacency formation is the process by which two OSPF routers negotiate enough shared parameters to exchange routing information. A stable adjacency reaches Full state and allows DBD, LSAs, and subsequent SPF work to proceed. Common causes of failure include mismatched area IDs, mismatched authentication (type or keys), different network types (for example one side thinking it's point-to-point while the other is broadcast), hello and dead timer mismatches, MTU differences, and subnet misconfiguration. When a neighbor is stuck in states such as Init, 2-Way, or ExStart, check these exact parameters. A concrete example: if R1 and R2 are connected on ge-0/0/0.0 and R1 has hello-interval 5 while R2 uses 10, R2 will see inconsistent timing and the adjacency may never progress to Full. A common misconception is to assume interface up/down is enough; a link can be up at L2 but still fail adjacency due to timer or MTU mismatch. To diagnose, run show ospf neighbor and show ospf interface detail to compare states and configured parameters. After you identify the mismatch, change one parameter, commit, and verify; avoid multiple simultaneous changes. What single mismatch would you check first on a flapping adjacency?

A reliable troubleshooting workflow begins with a small set of show commands that reveal OSPF state from different perspectives. Start with show ospf neighbor to confirm which neighbors exist and their states; a neighbor not in Full signals a problem. Then run show ospf interface detail to inspect hello and dead intervals, network type, cost, authentication, and MTU on that interface. Use show ospf database to validate LSAs and confirm whether expected router, network, summary, or external LSAs are present; filtering by LSA type narrows the view. Next, show route protocol ospf reveals what routes the router installed from OSPF and their metrics, which helps confirm whether SPF produced the expected result. Finally, show ospf statistics helps you detect packet-level issues such as missing or excessive hello or LSAs. A concrete example: when you suspect an adjacency failure between R1 and R2, run show ospf neighbor repeatedly to see state progression, then use show ospf interface detail to compare the configured hello-interval on both ends. Keep output capture or logs and correlate timestamps. A common mistake is to only check the routing table; always verify neighbors and database consistency first.

Traceoptions lets you log detailed OSPF activity to a file on Junos, including hello events, LSA processing, packet exchange, and state changes. Use traceoptions when show commands and monitor traffic do not reveal the timing or content of problem events. A safe workflow: configure a small file size and limited flags, reproduce the issue or wait for it to occur, review the log with show log, then delete the traceoptions configuration. Example configuration steps show how to limit impact: set protocols ospf traceoptions file ospf-debug size 1m files 2, then enable specific flags such as hello, lsa, packet, error, or state. After collecting logs, run show log ospf-debug and inspect timestamps and messages that indicate hello mismatches, dropped packets, or SPF recalculations. Remember that leaving traceoptions enabled can consume C P U and disk, so always remove them after verification. A common misconception is that more flags are always better; in production, prefer targeted flags to avoid overwhelming logs. When you do enable extensive tracing in a lab or maintenance window, monitor C P U and log size. What specific flag would you enable first to confirm hello interval problems?

When log messages do not reveal the problem, a packet capture on the interface lets you observe the actual OSPF packets exchanged. Junos monitor traffic interface detail can capture live packets similar to a tcpdump. You can filter for OSPF so you only see hellos, database description packets, and LSAs. For example, monitor traffic interface ge-0/0/0.0 no-resolve layer-2-headers matching "ospf" will show you whether hellos are being transmitted and which neighbor addresses they contain. Use this to verify that timers, authentication, and source addresses are correct from both ends. After capturing, stop the monitor and correlate packet timestamps with show logs to form a full timeline. LSA flooding is how OSPF distributes topology information. Routers flood LSAs within an area so each router maintains a consistent link-state database. Problems occur when some routers do not receive LSAs or have stale LSAs, producing inconsistent LSDBs and different SPF results. Symptoms include missing summary or external routes on some routers, or asymmetric path choices. Diagnosis starts with show ospf database and filtering by LSA type to see if expected router, network, summary, or external LSAs are present. Compare the LSDB on two neighbors for the same LSAs and sequence numbers; an older sequence number suggests the LSA did not flood correctly. An example: if an ASBR advertises an external LSA but some internal routers lack that LSA, run show ospf database external on multiple routers to find where flooding stopped. A misconception is to assume that a single missing route in the routing table is a distribution problem; first confirm whether the LSDB itself is inconsistent. Fourth, minimize the number of ABRs and ASBRs when possible; each adds SPF and LSDB complexity. Fifth, avoid virtual links unless necessary, and document their temporary nature. Sixth, summarize routes at ABRs to reduce LSDB size and SPF overhead, particularly in large networks. Seventh, document all OSPF design decisions, interface costs, priorities, and timer changes so future engineers can reproduce and audit configurations. Finally, always remove traceoptions and temporary monitoring configurations after troubleshooting to preserve device resources. A misconception is that adding more ABRs automatically improves resilience; instead, each ABR increases the domain's complexity.
